title: In the midst of life (1662)
hook: the burial service: in the midst of life we are in death
tomorrow: what if prayer is closer to hanging out than to a speech?

segments.voice: Yesterday the collect asked for a peace that can come before the trouble leaves. Yesterday's line: peace the world cannot give.

Funerals now come in more than one style. Some are called a celebration of life, with slideshows, favorite songs and laughter. Others keep the older shape: dark clothes, slow music, tears allowed. The 1662 prayer book has words for the graveside itself, said as the body is made ready to be laid in the earth: "In the midst of life we are in death." That's what it gives people to say at the edge of a grave. And Christians don't all lean on it the same way.
screen: `A CELEBRATION OF LIFE?` → `OR THE OLDER SHAPE?` → `IN THE MIDST OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole sentence, from the Burial of the Dead: "In the midst of life we are in death: of whom may we seek for succour, but of thee, O Lord, who for our sins art justly displeased?" Not at the end of life; in the middle of it. Then, at once, a question that holds its own answer: who can we go to for help? Thee. Two voices lean on this service differently. The first says: name death plainly. Keep it in view, as a psalm asks: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." Grief gets room, and nobody hurries past the grave. The second voice says: lead with hope. The same service reads Paul's letter to the Corinthians, with its taunt: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" So celebrate the life, and sing. Each has a best case. The first: hope that skips the grief rings hollow to the people grieving. The second: grief without hope forgets what the service is for. And the service holds both in one handful of earth, said as it falls on the coffin: "earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust; in sure and certain hope of the Resurrection to eternal life."
screen: `NOT AT THE END; IN THE MIDDLE.` · `FIRST VOICE: NAME IT PLAINLY.` · `SECOND VOICE: LEAD WITH HOPE.` · `DUST AND HOPE, ONE BREATH.` · then, large: `IN THE MIDST OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing that won't last: a cut flower, a fallen leaf, a candle, a photo of someone who has died. Let your eyes rest on it without pressing any thought hard. If someone you loved has died, you can say their name softly; if you pray, the psalm's line is there: so teach us to number our days.
In the midst of life. The graveside line that names death, then turns at once to ask God for help.
screen: `IN THE MIDST OF LIFE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Here's your line: in the midst of life, where dust and hope share one handful of earth. Go gently.

howItsDone: In the 1662 Book of Common Prayer these words are said or sung at the graveside; Anglican and Episcopal funerals still use them or later versions, and some Christian funerals are planned as a celebration of life.
